title: From Cricket Bat to Shotgun: At 50, Mairaj Ahmad Khan Chases Asian Games Glory
excerpt: India's first Olympic skeet shooter — a former Uttar Pradesh cricketer who once batted alongside a young Virender Sehwag — heads to Aichi-Nagoya for his fourth Asian Games, still chasing a first Asiad medal.
body:
• Mairaj Ahmad Khan, 50, will be the second-oldest member of India's contingent at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games — behind equestrian Shruti Vora — competing at his fourth Asian Games.
  • A former Uttar Pradesh and Jamia Millia Islamia cricketer who batted alongside a young Virender Sehwag, he switched to skeet full-time in 1999.
  • The first Indian to qualify for the Olympics in skeet (Rio 2016; Tokyo 2020 too), he won India's first individual skeet World Cup gold at Changwon in 2022.
  • He missed the Jakarta 2018 and Hangzhou 2022 Asian Games by narrow margins and arrives in Japan chasing a first Asiad medal; shotgun events begin September 21 in Toyota City.

The oldest rookie in the room

There was a time when Mairaj Ahmad Khan dreamed of making it big with a cricket bat. More than three decades later, the 50-year-old is still chasing sporting glory — only now with a shotgun in his grip. At the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which open September 19, he will be the second-oldest member of the Indian contingent, behind equestrian Shruti Vora, competing at his fourth continental games. "I am just going as a new shooter," he said with a laugh.

Khan missed the Jakarta 2018 and Hangzhou 2022 Asian Games by narrow margins — "I lost the berth by a close margin" — and arrives in Japan still hunting a first Asiad medal after finishing fifth at Incheon 2014.

A cricket career that almost was

"I was playing cricket when it all started in 1994," Khan recalls. A left-handed top-order batter, he represented Uttar Pradesh in the CK Nayudu and Vinoo Mankad Trophy competitions before joining Jamia Millia Islamia in 1996, playing inter-university cricket and the Vizzy Trophy. Among his university teammates was a young Virender Sehwag: "I have played with Sehwag and done a lot of nets with him. He played just one match with us because he went on to play for India that year."

Guns were not unfamiliar — his zamindar family from Khurja, in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district, had always kept firearms. As a youngster he tried air rifle and .22 rifle shooting, winning Rs 30 at a district event in Bulandshahr. "I bought a cricket bat with that money," he laughed.

The shoot-off that changed everything

The pivot came in Delhi, where weekends with a cousin — a Group Captain in the Indian Air Force — led Khan to tag along to the Nationals at the Karni Singh Shooting Range. The range buzzed with legends like Asian Games gold medallist Raja Randhir Singh and Olympian Gurbir Singh. "I felt very fascinated by the sport," he says.

A year later, relatives returning from a shooting pre-Nationals told him they had qualified — and Khan entered his name for the next year. He dabbled in trap and skeet until 1999, when a Chennai competition forced the choice: a skeet shoot-off against Ronjan Sodhi, the future Asian Games gold medallist and Khel Ratna awardee. "I missed the first double shots. I thought he would win. But he also could not shoot both his targets. In the next round, I went on to win." That victory settled it: "After that, skeet became my life. I never picked up the trap gun again."

What he built with a shotgun

The decision transformed his life. In 2016, Khan became the first Indian ever to qualify for the Olympics in skeet, finishing ninth in qualification at Rio; he competed again at Tokyo 2020. In 2022 at Changwon he won India's first individual ISSF World Cup gold in men's skeet — a comeback after his father's death in 2021, the COVID disruption and lost sponsorship nearly pushed him into retirement. "I realised that maybe this is the time to say thank you to the sport," he recalled — then self-funded his return to Korea and won.

He has been coached by Andrea Benelli, Sunny Thomas and now Riccardo Filippelli, runs the MAK Shooting Foundation NGO for young talent, and once coached Angad Vir Singh Bajwa. For Aichi-Nagoya he trained at a 15-day shotgun camp at Delhi's Karni Singh Range with S&C coaches, physios and head coach Amrinder Singh Cheema. "If you go into a competition with fewer expectations, it is better for you," he told SAI Media. "If you go with expectations, you are already in the future; you are not in the present."

Diaspora angle

Nothing captures Khan's longevity like the 35-year gap between him and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the 15-year-old cricket sensation and youngest member of India's contingent. "When I started shooting, he would have been born around that time," Khan said. Asked for advice for the teenager, he laughed: "Fifty is the new 20, you know. He has youth, but I have experience."

"Unke andar josh hai aur mere andar hosh hai. He has the passion. I have the wisdom."

— Mairaj Ahmad Khan

What to watch

The shotgun events begin September 21 in Toyota City. A first Asiad medal at 50 would complete an already historic CV — and Khan is not done: he missed Paris 2024 but has his sights on Los Angeles 2028, where a third Olympic appearance at 52 would make him one of India's oldest Olympians. "I take one day at a time. I take one target at a time," he says.
image_caption: Skeet shooter Mairaj Ahmad Khan. The 50-year-old will compete at his fourth Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, still chasing a first Asiad medal.
nri_angle: A longevity story that resonates with diaspora sports fans — and a reminder of the unconventional pathways India's veteran athletes still carve at the highest level.
